old_title: France protests latest: Shops boarded up as 70,000 police brace for riots
new_title: More than 1000 arrested as protesters clash with police in Paris

Luxury shops in France boarded up windows and added guards, while some of its top tourist attractions and metro stations closed, ahead of protests on Saturday, after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.
The Louvre, Musée d'Orsay and the Opera House will remain closed throughout Saturday as authorities fear renewed violence, with 70,000 police officers deployed across the country.
Some shopkeepers have begun arming themselves with baseball bats, crowbars and shotguns to protect their businesses.
French president Emmanuel Macron met with high school unions yesterday in an 11th hour attempt to quell unrest anticipated over the weekend.
However, student leaders emerged from the talks dissatisfied, urging pupils to continue protesting until the government presented concrete proposals to address their demands.
"We are not satisfied," said Nathanael Combary, president of the campaign group High School Renewal, calling on students to maintain a "standoff" with the government ahead of further talks with the prime minister on Monday.
The demonstrations, which began over deteriorating conditions in schools, have spread across France, fuelled by wider anger over rising living costs and strained public services.
What to know about the weapons and tactics blamed for injuring French protesters
The European cities facing more protests from Paris to Milan as cost of living crisis bites
Violent protests have broken out across Europe amid growing frustration over the cost of living crisis, a lack of affordable housing and deteriorating conditions in schools.
As many as 550,000 people turned out across France last Saturday, according to authorities, to demonstrate against declining public services. Protests turned violent in Paris as shops were looted and cars set on fire in some of the city's worst violence in years.
France is now bracing for another weekend of unrest, despite curfews imposed across the country and an 11th hour meeting between president Emmanuel Macron and high school unions on Friday to hear out their concerns and demands.
France mounts huge security operation as protesters prepare to march
French security forces fanned out across Paris on Saturday ahead of protests that authorities fear could turn violent, with interior minister Laurent Nunez urging police to be "hyper-reactive" against troublemakers and looters.
Soldiers from an anti-terrorism military unit patrolled the Champs-Elysees avenue while police vans circled the Arc de Triomphe, looking to protect some of the capital's most famous sites from any repeat of the unrest that shook France last week.
Nunez has mobilised 70,000 police nationwide for Saturday's demonstrations, 10,000 more than on 17 October, when a wave of vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
Anger over living costs and strained public services has drawn students, workers and unions onto the streets in recent weeks, but authorities say radical militants and bands of young looters have exploited the protests to sow chaos. Speaking to police in Paris, Nunez warned officers that they would face attempts to target shops, public institutions and security forces.
"We have to be ultra, ultra responsive. We have significant calls for disruption `from political groups and quite simply from criminals," he said. "It is going to be a long day."
Watch live: France braces for another weekend of protests as 70,000 police deployed
Louvre shuts down over fears of violence in Paris
The Louvre is closed on Saturday, along with several other major Paris museums, because of concerns about potential violence during planned protests, France's culture ministry says.
The Orsay and Picasso museums are also among those that are closed, the ministry said.
The ministry called on all institutions under its authority to adopt any necessary measures to ensure "visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks".
The closures follow protests last Saturday that descended into mayhem, with rioters setting fires, smashing shop windows, looting and clashing with police.
Trump questions NFL's decision to go ahead with Paris game
President Donald Trump has questioned the NFL's decision to go ahead with a game in Paris amid widespread unrest in the country.
The first regular-season NFL game to be staged in France is due to kick off on Sunday at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, which sits just north of Paris.
Trump said Friday that the league "could have probably postponed" the fixture between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints.
France's luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.
France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.
But some decided staying open was too risky after last week's events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux.
A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital's famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.
Staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren't taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighbourhood is also planned.
Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.
Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.
Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests.
"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said.
What sparked the fiery protests in France - and how they are spreading across Europe
Demonstrations were boosted by other groups last week, protesting the high cost of living and what they say is the deterioration of the social welfare system.
The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), which is one of the country's largest unions, backed the protests, issuing a call for lower prices and higher pensions and wages.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets. Protesters in Marseille stormed the town hall, painting an 'A' for anarchy on a wall, while in Paris, police fired tear gas and a water cannon and rioters threw stones and fireworks.
In Lyon, protesters set fire to the city's tourism office.
French authorities said there were more than 500,000 protesters across the country, with more than 800 arrests in Paris alone.
Macron has called for calm, saying "we all feel anger and shame" after "unprecedented violence" nationwide. He vowed to "make examples if need be" of the rioters, warning for "those who want to spark violence and create unrest in our country, we will not yield".
Fears of further violence as France braces for more protests this weekend
France is bracing for more protests this weekend after a week of turmoil and upheaval across the country following riots and looting last weekend.
The country has faced unprecedented violence after student protests led to clashes with police, which caused at least one teenager to have his hand blown off by a stun grenade and a one-year-old child to be hospitalised after a firework went off near his pram.
Justice minister Gerald Darmanin said that at least 217 people had been jailed in connection with the violence over the last week after undergoing fast-track trials to curtail the disorder.
Police deployments are also to be increased by 20 per cent, according to the country's interior minister, Jean-Didier Berger.
But President Emmanuel Macron said that this weekend's demonstrations will be strictly limited to those organised by authorised unions.

Mass rallies drew hundreds of thousands of protesters across France on Saturday, with predominantly peaceful demonstrations giving way to evening skirmishes in Paris and Marseille despite an extensive security strategy deployed to head off a repeat of the previous week's unrest.
According to the interior ministry, 410,000 individuals joined demonstrations nationwide, though trade unions claimed the actual turnout was double that figure.
The main demonstration happened on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested as officers faced "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" people, interior minister Laurent Nunez claimed.
Two people were "seriously" injured, Mr Nunez said, with one man injured in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
The protests began in mid-September, when secondary school pupils took to the streets over staff shortages, deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms. The movement has since grown into a broader challenge to Emmanuel Macron's government, drawing in teachers, parents and trade unions.
Conditions turned hostile following the conclusion of the rally on Saturday. Riot police deployed tear gas and water cannon against a crowd of roughly 500 masked youths, who eventually dispersed in the cold, wet conditions.
In Marseille, France's second city, young protesters set fire to rubbish bins to obstruct roads and threw stones and bottles at security officers. Police reported that several businesses, including two jewellery shops, were looted.
Confrontations were also reported in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.
"In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Mr Nunez, who blamed far-left activists and organised criminal groups for provoking the unrest.
Mr Nunez said 135 people had been arrested before the main marches began, with police seizing an assortment of weapons, including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, improvised weapons, a katana sword and airsoft guns. Paris police later reported that 65 people had been arrested in the capital.
The demonstrations come as Macron approaches the final months of his presidency, with the growing movement exposing wider anger over living costs, public services and the government's handling of dissent.
Security measures in the capital
A total of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed by authorities - 10,000 more than the preceding week - after officials admitted they had underestimated the extent of the unrest on 17 October.
Mr Nunez stated to reporters that the violence was less severe than the previous week, when vandals and looters engaged in widespread destruction. "What changed was anticipation," he said.
He added that far-right activists had attempted to confront leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, creating a potential new dimension to the disorder.
Large parts of central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, with business owners shuttering premises, museums closing and more than 20 metro stations suspended.
Trade associations urged shopkeepers to keep their doors closed following damage or looting at thousands of commercial premises across France the previous weekend.
"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
A number of the capital's prominent cultural locations, such as the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, opted to close as a preventative measure, leaving visitors disappointed.
"Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
Protest movement spreads
The countrywide movement originated from minor student demonstrations in the Paris suburbs last month over school conditions. It quickly expanded into broader opposition to government economic policies, prompting similar rallies in neighbouring European nations.
Belgian police used pepper spray and tear gas during confrontations in Brussels with anti-government protesters on Saturday, while demonstrations also took place across several Italian cities for a second consecutive weekend, as well as in Albania.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the Paris demonstration, suggested that rallies would persist until President Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends next year, addresses social discontent in France, one of the world's wealthiest nations.
"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.
Far-right event underway
Numerous protesters accused the administration of an excessive response to the prior week's disruption, noting that military personnel were assigned to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a famous boulevard featuring high-end shops and restaurants.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.
The day's initial approved march proceeded without incident in Orléans, roughly 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where marchers gathered to oppose Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.
Tensions were heightened by a shooting west of Paris on Friday, in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one individual and injured four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.
